opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to what the story of AI progress looks like from the outside. When people think about breakthroughs, they picture a clever new idea: someone comes up with a new architecture or a new training objective, writes a paper, and suddenly everything changes. That's a very compelling narrative, and it's the part that gets cited and talked about.

But when you're actually inside a lab training large models, a huge share of what determines whether you succeed is engineering. Can you get your training run to work efficiently across thousands of accelerators? Can you find the bug that's silently making your loss curve slightly worse? Can you build infrastructure that lets researchers run experiments quickly and trust the results? A lot of the progress we've seen has come from taking relatively simple ideas and scaling them up, and scaling is mostly an engineering problem.

There's also a feedback loop. If your infrastructure is good, you can run many more experiments, so research goes faster. If it's bad, even the best researcher gets stuck waiting on jobs or chasing down issues that turn out to be a broken data pipeline rather than a flaw in their idea. So in practice the line between research and engineering is blurry, and often the people with the most impact are the ones who can do both: understand the ML well enough to know what matters, and write the code that makes it work at scale.

I think historically, especially in academia, there was a status hierarchy where research was seen as the prestigious part and engineering as support work. That made people, including people interested in AI safety, assume they needed a PhD and a strong publication record to contribute. My view is that strong software engineers can often have a very large impact at frontier labs, sometimes larger than they'd expect, and I'd encourage people with that background to take that path seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says academia had a status hierarchy that treated research as prestigious and engineering as support work.

r002.rationale: It says progress has involved scaling relatively simple ideas up and that scaling is mostly an engineering problem, connecting model scaling with engineering's importance.

r003.rationale: It mentions training across thousands of accelerators, but does not compare the engineering complexity of that work with inexpensive small-model experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few things going on. One is just that research is more legible from the outside. When a lab publishes a paper, the thing people see is the idea, the new architecture or the new training objective, and the name on the paper. What they don't see is the eighteen months of work it took to build a distributed training system that could actually run the experiment at scale without falling over, or the person who spent weeks tracking down why one in every few thousand batches was producing NaNs. So the narrative that gets told is "someone had a clever idea," when the reality is that the clever idea was maybe ten percent of the work.

The second thing is that a lot of people come to AI from academia, where the constraint really was ideas. You had a small compute budget, you had a few GPUs, and the question was what's the most interesting thing you can do with them. That selects for valuing novel ideas very highly. But once you move into the regime where you're training very large models, the constraints flip. You usually have a pretty good sense of what to try. The bottleneck is whether you can actually execute it: can you get the model to train stably, can you make your infrastructure efficient enough that the experiment finishes this month instead of next quarter, can you build the evaluations that tell you whether it worked. Those are fundamentally engineering problems.

And honestly, I think the distinction is a bit artificial at this point. The best researchers I've worked with are extremely strong engineers, and a lot of what looks like research progress is really someone noticing that if you fix a bug or restructure a pipeline, suddenly a result that didn't work before now works. In my own experience, I came in thinking I'd be doing something that looked like research in the academic sense, and the majority of my time ended up being writing code, debugging, and making systems work. And I think that's the normal case, not the exception.

So when people are deciding what to work on, or what to learn, I'd push back on the instinct that you need to be the person with the brilliant idea to matter. If you're a strong software engineer who can work on hard systems problems, you're probably more useful to most AI projects right now than a lot of people imagine, and the field has underweighted that for a long time.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research is more visible and that academia selects for valuing ideas, but does not attribute the overvaluation to research having greater prestige.

r002.rationale: It says that with very large models the constraints flip and execution becomes the bottleneck, emphasizing stable training and efficient infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It contrasts small academic compute budgets with large-model training and mentions distributed systems, but does not clearly state that large-cluster training requires more complex engineering than inexpensive small-model experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that research is the most visible part of progress. You see a paper with a new idea, and it’s natural to attribute the improvement to that idea. You don’t see all the work that went into making the experiments run reliably, getting the data right, or making the system efficient enough that you could try more things.

And those engineering improvements compound. If you can run experiments twice as fast, you get more chances to discover something. If your infrastructure is reliable, you can trust the results and spend less time debugging. So engineering isn’t just implementing something after the research is done. It changes what research you’re able to do.

I think people sometimes picture the bottleneck as someone having a brilliant insight, when it can be turning a fairly straightforward idea into something that actually works at scale. That takes a lot of engineering judgment, and it’s harder to capture in a paper or give one person credit for.

r001.rationale: The response explains overvaluation through research being more visible and easier to credit; it does not attribute it to research having greater prestige.

r002.rationale: It says engineering affects what research can be done and mentions making ideas work at scale, but does not state that scaling AI models increased engineering’s importance.

r003.rationale: It does not compare compute-intensive training on large distributed clusters with inexpensive small-model experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that research is the most visible part of the process. You see a paper with a new idea, and it’s natural to attribute the progress to that idea. You don’t see all the work that went into making the experiments reliable, getting the system to run efficiently, or making it easy to test the next idea.

But those things really determine how quickly you can make progress. If you can run twice as many experiments, or trust your results more, that can be enormously valuable. And often the bottleneck isn’t that nobody has a promising idea. It’s that implementing it and finding out whether it works is difficult.

So I think the distinction can be misleading. Good engineering isn’t just taking something the researchers have already figured out and putting it into production. It’s part of how you figure things out in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says research is more visible, but does not attribute its overvaluation to greater prestige.

r002.rationale: It discusses engineering’s role in progress but does not state that scaling AI models increased engineering’s importance.

r003.rationale: It mentions making systems run efficiently, but does not compare the engineering demands of large distributed training with inexpensive small-model experiments.
